subject: Agriculture
title: Harvest Loss and Storage
description: A short lesson to help you apply Harvest Loss and Storage.

hook.text: One-third of food produced globally is lost or wasted. In developing countries, most loss happens after harvest.

buildup.text: Without proper storage, grain is eaten by insects, contaminated by mold, or spoiled by moisture.

discovery.text: Hermetic storage bags—airtight bags that suffocate insects—have cut post-harvest losses by 98% in field trials.

twist.text: A $2 storage bag can save $50 worth of grain. The economics are obvious—distribution is the challenge.

climax.text: Reducing post-harvest loss could feed 1 billion more people without planting a single extra acre.

punchline.text: We don't only need to grow more. We need to lose less.

quiz.question: How do hermetic storage bags prevent grain loss?

details.summary: Harvest loss and storage failures destroy an estimated 14% of global food production after crops leave the field. This topic covers mechanical damage during harvest, post-harvest spoilage, pest infestations in storage, and technologies that reduce these losses.
details.whyItMatters: Reducing post-harvest losses is one of the most cost-effective ways to increase food supply without farming more land, using more water, or adding more fertilizer.
takeaways: Sub-Saharan Africa loses up to 40% of some crops between harvest and consumption
Hermetic storage bags eliminate insect damage without chemicals for smallholders
Cold chain infrastructure is critical for reducing fruit and vegetable spoilage

faq.question: What causes the most post-harvest food loss globally?
faq.answer: In developing countries, inadequate drying, poor storage facilities, insect and rodent damage, and lack of cold chains cause the most loss. In developed countries, losses occur more from market standards, overproduction, and retail-level waste.

faq.question: How can small farmers reduce post-harvest grain losses?
faq.answer: Affordable technologies like hermetic storage bags seal grain in airtight containers that suffocate insects without chemicals. Proper drying before storage, improved silos, and solar-powered dryers also significantly reduce losses.
